blocks.text: Dear Ms. Ward:

It was a pleasure to talk through the coming year's portfolio questions with you last month, and this letter is meant to set down, plainly and in one place, the terms on which our firm will carry out that work for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}; once you have read it and signed the copy enclosed for the purpose, it will stand as the agreement between us. I have written it at some length and in ordinary language, because you are entitled to understand exactly what you are committing your firm to rather than to infer it, and I would ask that you read what follows against the conversation we had and tell me, before you countersign, if anything set out here departs from what you understood us to have agreed.
The Scope of the Engagement

What we have undertaken is a portfolio strategy review for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}, by which I mean a considered examination of the businesses the firm holds, of the returns and the demands each of them places on the whole, and of the question of where the firm's capital and attention are best directed over the period ahead. We will describe the portfolio as it now stands, weigh each part of it on its own merits and against the others, and set out a recommendation together with the reasoning that leads to it, so that where you come to differ from our view you can see precisely at which point your judgment and ours part company. The work covers our analysis and our counsel; it does not extend to carrying out whatever you decide, nor does it constitute legal, tax, or accounting advice, on which you should continue to rely on the advisers who ordinarily provide it to you.
How We Mean to Work

Our manner is deliberate, and I would rather describe it to you now than have it come as a surprise once we have begun. We start by learning how the firm actually operates and what each business is asked to contribute before we commit any judgment to paper; we test what we are told against evidence we can gather for ourselves; and we bring you our thinking as it forms rather than holding it back for a single unveiling at the close, so that the conclusions, when they arrive, contain nothing you are meeting for the first time. Where the evidence will not carry a firm conclusion we will say so, and say what it would take to reach one, because an assessment that overstates its own certainty is of no use to a firm that must act on it.
The People You Will Be Working With

The day-to-day work will be carried out by two of our research staff, whom you will come to know well. Steven Hunt will assemble the market and company evidence that frames the review and will be your most frequent point of contact on questions of data and scheduling; he is quick and resourceful, and candid about the places where the evidence is thinner than one would like. Melissa Casey will build the exhibits and hold the analysis together from one working session to the next, and she is exacting about sources and labels in a way that repays the attention. I will keep my own hand on the judgments that decide how far a conclusion can be pressed before it outruns what supports it, and nothing will leave the firm under our name without my having read it first.
Our Fee and When We Begin

Our fee for the engagement as I have described it is {{fact:f:E-2019-002.fee}}, fixed for the scope set out above and covering the time of the people named in it. The work will begin on {{fact:f:E-2019-002.start}} and is expected to run for something on the order of nine months, though we will treat it as finished when the work is genuinely done rather than when the calendar says that it ought to be. Should you ask us to widen the work materially beyond what this letter contemplates, I will raise the question of the fee with you and we will settle it together before that further work begins, so that nothing ever reaches you on an invoice you have not agreed to in advance.
Invoicing and Payment

We will render invoices against the fixed fee as the work proceeds rather than in a single sum at the close, and each invoice will be payable within thirty days of your receipt of it. The fee does not include incidental costs such as travel or the reproduction of materials; those we will incur only with your agreement and pass through to you at what they cost us, itemized so that no line on an invoice is a matter of guesswork.
Duration and Ending the Engagement

Either of us may bring the engagement to an end on fourteen days' written notice to the other, for any reason or for none, and I would far rather you felt free to exercise that liberty than continue with work you had ceased to find useful. Should you be the one to end it, you will owe us for the work properly performed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and for nothing beyond that.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}} in the course of this work we will hold in confidence and use only for the purposes of the engagement, an obligation that binds each member of the team, that survives the end of our involvement, and that extends to the fact of the engagement as fully as to its substance. We ask the same of you in respect of the written materials and the methods we share with you, which are the firm's own and are given for your use rather than for wider circulation.
The Limit of Our Liability

We will carry out the work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of a firm engaged for it, and we stand behind what we do. We do not, however, govern the decision you will ultimately take or the conditions under which you will act on it, and so, except to the extent the law does not permit such a limit, our liability to you arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be resolved by the courts of that state. Should any single provision of this letter be held unenforceable, the remainder of it will continue in force, unaffected by that provision's failure.

If this letter reflects the understanding we reached, I would ask that you sign the enclosed copy where indicated below and return it to me, keeping the other for your own file; the one step needed on your side is that signature, and once it is in hand Steven Hunt will write to you within the week to arrange the first meetings and set out the initial requests for information, so that we lose no time in beginning.

We are engaged to help {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}} decide where the firm's capital and attention are best directed across its portfolio over the year ahead. The client wants a recommendation their leadership can act on, grounded in evidence rather than a survey of every option. This memo sets down what we are trying to produce and who owns which part of it, so that we begin in step instead of converging on it later.

The engagement began on {{fact:f:E-2019-002.start}}, and our sponsor on the client side is Barbara Ward, the Director of Operations, who has agreed to clear our path to the data and the people we will need. Any request of substance to the client goes through her, and I will hold the running list of what we have asked for so that it stays on one channel.

The first weeks have one job, and it is a narrow one. We build a shared and sourced picture of the portfolio as it stands before we form any view on where it should go. We do not draft conclusions yet; those come later, and only once the facts they rest on are settled and agreed with the client.

The end product is a written recommendation on the portfolio with the workpapers standing behind it, and everything in the plan below feeds one or the other. It is worth saying plainly that we are advising the decision, not making it: the choice remains the client's, and we keep our analysis and our recommendation clearly apart so their leadership can weigh the evidence before being handed the answer.
How the work divides

items: Portfolio and market evidence. I take the market and competitive read, so we can place each business against what its market is actually doing, and I hand off each figure with its source attached.

Exhibits and the analytical pack. Melissa Casey owns the exhibits and keeps the pack consistent from one working session to the next, on the standing principle that an unsourced chart is an unfinished one.

Internal reconciliation. Melissa Casey leads the reconciliation of the client's own numbers across the businesses, so that when the comparison is drawn no one has to argue about the denominator after the fact.
Data requests. Every request to the client routes through one list rather than several; I keep it current so that Barbara Ward is never asked twice for the same thing.
The engagement file. We open a shared file this week and put sources into it as they arrive, so that any figure we later rely on can be traced back to where it came from.

blocks.text: The first week

The priority this week is access. I will send the client our first data request by the end of the week, and Melissa Casey will begin the market and portfolio scan in parallel so that we are not idle while the data comes back. Before we meet again, I would ask you for two things: the documents your side of the work will need from the client, and the people you would want to interview; send both to me by Friday and I will fold them into the single request.

From next week we hold a short standing check-in between the two of us before anything goes to the client, kept to status, blockers, and what we still need from them. That keeps our requests to the client on one channel and their answers on the record, which matters more on an engagement of this length than it may seem at the outset.

I will circulate a short index of what has arrived and what is still outstanding, and refresh it as things move, so that no one has to ask me twice for the same status and so the picture we carry into each check-in with Barbara Ward is an accurate one.
Dear Barbara,

The portfolio strategy work for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}} is moving on schedule, and I wanted to line up the last of the data we need before the picture goes any wider. We have the market and competitive read well under way, and Melissa Casey has finished a first pass on the business-by-business profiles, which are holding up against what we heard from you at the outset.

The gap now is on the internal numbers. Three of the schedules we asked for, the ones behind the two largest of the businesses, have not yet reached us, and without them Melissa Casey cannot close the comparison across the portfolio. If you can have them to us by the middle of next week, we can keep the review on its timeline rather than presenting around a hole in it.

I would also like to hold a short working session to walk you through what the read is showing before we take it any further. For that session I have you, Barbara Ward, Melissa Casey, and myself, Steven Hunt; let me know a day next week that suits you and I will hold it and send a short agenda round once the date is fixed.
Sincerely,
Working Session Minutes: Portfolio Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}

These minutes record the working session held to review the state of the portfolio strategy work for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}} and to fix what each party carries forward from here; they are intended as the shared record the team works from, and any attendee who reads a point differently should say so within the week so that the record can be corrected before it is relied on.
Present

items: Steven Hunt, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Melissa Casey, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Barbara Ward, Director of Operations, {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}

blocks.text: Matters discussed

Steven Hunt opened by taking the group through the market and competitive read as it now stands, setting out for each of the larger businesses how its market has moved over the recent period and where the demand behind it appears to be settling, and he was careful to distinguish the parts of that read that rest on external data from the parts that still rest on our own estimate, so that no one in the room left more confident than the evidence yet allows.

We then reviewed the business-by-business profiles I have been assembling, and we agreed that the shape of the portfolio is clearer than it was at the outset while several of the internal figures remain to be reconciled, in particular the cost allocations across the two largest businesses, which we cannot close until the client's finance team supplies the schedules behind them; until those arrive, the comparison across the portfolio carries a wider band than we would want to place in front of anyone.

On method, we agreed to hold each figure in the profiles to a stated source before it is used, and to keep what we know apart from what we assume, marking every estimate as an estimate with the band around it; this discipline slows the assembly somewhat, but it is what will let the client's own people rerun the comparison after we have gone, which Barbara Ward noted her leadership would expect to be able to do.

Barbara Ward gave the client's account of where the outstanding schedules stand and undertook to have them to us by the middle of next month, and, before we set an action against that, she walked us through two reorganizations within the period that explain part of the discrepancy we had flagged in the earlier numbers; we agreed that the profiles would note those reorganizations plainly rather than smooth over the discontinuity they create in the figures.
Actions agreed

rows: Deliver the cost-allocation schedules for the two largest businesses
Close the portfolio comparison once the schedules are in
Firm up the market and competitive read and tie each figure to its source
Note the two reorganizations in the affected business profiles

blocks.text: We will reconvene once the schedules are in hand and the portfolio comparison has been closed against them, and I will circulate these minutes to the group today; unless a correction reaches me within the week, they will stand as the agreed record of the session.
Status Report: Portfolio Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}

Prepared for the leadership of {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}} by the Calderwood engagement team, covering the period since our last update and looking ahead to the work that follows. The team on your engagement is Steven Hunt, who assembles the market and portfolio evidence, and Melissa Casey, who builds the analysis and the exhibits that carry it.
Where the engagement stands

The engagement is at its midpoint and on plan. The market and competitive read is substantially done, the business-by-business profiles are drafted, and the comparison across the portfolio is under way. One data dependency on your side, the cost-allocation schedules for the two largest businesses, is holding up the last of that comparison, and it is the item most worth your attention in the coming weeks.

The recommendation is not yet formed, and at this stage it should not be. We are still assembling and reconciling the evidence your leadership will need to weigh the portfolio with confidence, and we would rather bring you a narrow picture we can stand behind than a broad one we cannot. What follows is progress against the plan rather than conclusions drawn ahead of it.
What we completed this period

The bulk of this period went to the evidence base, and it is now far enough along to describe. We have held each figure to a source as we go, so that the comparison, when it closes, will rest on numbers your own people can trace and rerun rather than take on trust.

items: Steven Hunt completed the market and competitive read for each of the larger businesses, distinguishing throughout what rests on external data from what remains our own estimate.
The business-by-business profiles are drafted, and Melissa Casey has reconciled the internal figures for all but the two largest businesses, where the schedules are still outstanding.
The benchmark set against which the portfolio is weighed is built and checked against outside data, so the comparisons rest on figures we can defend.
We held a working session with your team and agreed how two reorganizations within the period will be reflected in the affected profiles rather than smoothed over.

blocks.text: A word on method, since it shapes what you can rely on. Every figure in the profiles carries a source in the engagement file, and where a number is our estimate rather than a settled fact it is labeled as an estimate, with the band around it; your finance owners can trace any line back to where it came from, and we would encourage them to do exactly that before your leadership sees the comparison.
What comes next

The next period turns on the cost-allocation schedules from your finance team. Once they are in hand, Melissa Casey closes the portfolio comparison and we finalize the profiles for the two largest businesses, so that the picture moves together rather than in pieces. With the comparison closed, we will bring your team a first view of how the portfolio sorts before any recommendation is drawn from it.

That first view comes ahead of the recommendation itself and is meant to be argued with, so that your leadership can steer the analysis while it is still open rather than react to it once it has hardened. We will bring it to the working session that follows the close of the comparison, and we would welcome your team's challenge to it there.
The engagement budget

The engagement is a fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-002.fee}}, and at its midpoint the work is tracking within it, with nothing in what remains that we expect to change that, provided the scope holds. Should you ask us to widen the work beyond the portfolio review as it was scoped, we would raise the fee with you and settle it before taking the further work on, as the engagement letter provides.
What we are watching

items: The outstanding cost-allocation schedules are the one real dependency. Until they arrive the portfolio comparison carries a wider band than we want, and if they slip much past next month the final read slips with them; we would tell you rather than quietly absorb the delay.

The two reorganizations within the period create a genuine discontinuity in the internal figures. That is a matter of record rather than a problem, but it will shape how some of the businesses compare, and we are flagging it now so that it does not land as a surprise later.
Nothing else on the engagement is off plan at this point.

blocks.text: We will send the next update after the working session that follows the close of the comparison. If anything here would be better discussed before then, Steven Hunt is your point of contact and will make the time.
Minutes of the Working Session: Portfolio Strategy for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}

These minutes set down what was reviewed and agreed at the working session on the portfolio strategy work for {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}, held to take stock now that the comparison across the portfolio has been closed and to agree how the remaining weeks are spent; as before, any attendee who reads a point otherwise should raise it within the week so that we correct the record together.
In attendance

items: Steven Hunt, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Melissa Casey, Research Associate, Calderwood Partners
Barbara Ward, Director of Operations, {{fact:f:E-2019-002.client}}

blocks.text: Summary of discussion

We began with the state of the completed comparison, and Steven Hunt took the group through how the portfolio now sorts once the cost-allocation schedules from the client are folded in, noting that the picture held broadly to the earlier read while sharpening it in the two places we had flagged as uncertain; we agreed that the two largest businesses now sit where the reconciled figures put them rather than where the earlier estimates had, and that the profiles should say as much plainly.

On method we held to the same discipline as before, keeping what the reconciled figures now show apart from what remains an estimate and marking each accordingly, since the value of the comparison to the client rests on their being able to rerun it after we have gone; Steven Hunt confirmed that every line in the closed comparison traces to a source in the engagement file, which is the condition we had set for treating it as settled.

We then worked through the options for the portfolio that the analysis supports, and rather than settle on one we set out the handful of criteria against which the client's leadership will weigh them, so that the choice reaches them as a set of reasoned alternatives and not as a single answer handed down; Barbara Ward was clear that her leadership would expect to see the reasoning behind each option, and we agreed that the reasoning would travel with the options rather than be held back for the recommendation.

Before closing we reviewed what remains, and I set out the state of the exhibits, which are largely built but not yet through a final check for sourcing and labels; we agreed that nothing would go in front of the client's leadership as settled until the underlying figures had been through both our review and the client's, and Barbara Ward undertook to line up the finance owners for that review in the coming weeks.
Actions carried forward

items: Steven Hunt to finalize the portfolio sort and confirm each figure against its source in the engagement file.
Melissa Casey to complete the final sourcing and labeling check on the exhibits before any of them are shown.
Barbara Ward to line up the client's finance owners to review the reconciled figures.
The team to prepare the portfolio options and their reasoning for the client leadership's review at the next session, ahead of any recommendation.

blocks.text: We will reconvene once the exhibits have cleared their final check and the client's review of the figures is arranged, and I will circulate these minutes to the group today; unless a correction reaches me within the week, they stand as the record of the session.
